title: Construction Profit Margin UK: What Good Looks Like
meta_description: What a good construction profit margin looks like in the UK, how gross, operating and net margins differ, and eight practical ways to improve yours.
h1: Construction Profit Margin UK: What Good Looks Like
hero_subtitle: A practical guide to knowing whether your margin is healthy or just survivable.

intro.answer: Construction profit margin is profit divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage. Use gross margin to review direct job costs, operating margin to include overheads, and net margin to see what remains after the other expenses in your accounts.

image.alt: A construction business owner reviewing profit margins

intro.roadmap: Start with a worked example, distinguish margin from markup, then use your own project and company figures to choose the next action.

briefing.title: Three Margins, Three Different Answers
briefing.intro: Owners often quote one margin figure and assume it describes the business. It does not. Each of the three answers a different question, and knowing which one you are looking at is the difference between a real diagnosis and a comfortable one.

panels.heading: What is the difference between the three margins?
paragraphs: Gross profit is revenue less direct costs. Gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue. Operating profit also deducts operating overheads; net profit includes the remaining income and expenses reported in your accounts.
A fall in gross margin can reflect pricing, cost overruns or the mix of work. If gross margin holds but operating profit falls, check overheads and revenue volume before deciding what to change.

panels.heading: Worked example: where did the profit go?
paragraphs: Illustrative figures, excluding VAT: £100,000 revenue less £60,000 direct costs gives £40,000 gross profit and a 40% gross margin. Deduct £20,000 operating overheads to get £20,000 operating profit, or 20%.
If interest and tax together are an assumed £10,000, net profit is £10,000, or 10%. The tax amount is an example, not a tax calculation or recommended target.
steps: Compare the quoted direct cost with actual cost and remaining cost to complete.
Identify whether labour, materials, variations or programme delays explain the gap.
Assign one corrective action, an owner and a review date.

review.label: Margin is not markup
review.text: £80,000 direct cost priced at £100,000 gives 20% gross margin but 25% markup on cost. Adding 20% to cost gives a £96,000 price and only 16.7% gross margin. Overheads still come out of gross profit.
